answer:
The talk changed over time: it was upbeat when the deal was announced in July 2000, defensive when it fell apart in March 2001, and critical in late 2001 and early 2002, when press clips described the Braveheart partnership. The Blockbuster count is 240 emails (mail_counts), peaking at 26 in June 2001 and 33 in October 2001. Much of the 2001–02 material is forwarded press or newsletters, and I label that below.

**Launch, mid-2000 (internal announcements)**
- On 19 July 2000, Enron Broadband Services announced a 20-year exclusive agreement with Blockbuster to deliver "entertainment on demand" to consumers.
- An EBS update in June had already listed it among "landmark long-term agreements" for video on demand.
- In September, an Enron staffer noted that Blockbuster and Enron had entered into an agreement with nCUBE to provide video streaming appliances and software.

**Trouble in the content, late 2000 to early 2001 (internal mail)**
- In November 2000, talking points for Vivendi's chairman said negotiations with Universal had stalled because Universal would not sign long-term agreements without Vivendi's support.
- Those talking points also said Blockbuster had refused to renew its Universal VHS/DVD agreement until Universal granted digital VOD rights.
- On 5 March 2001, a PR contact circulated standby statements that were "NONE OF THESE IS A NEWS RELEASE TO PROACTIVELY ISSUE."
- One of the three versions was for "if and when we cancel the contract," and she added that Blockbuster's CEO had said at a conference that Enron "won't extend the trial due to small movie selection."

**The split, 9 March 2001**
- Enron told employees it was discontinuing the exclusive relationship in order to build direct relationships with content providers and distribution partners.
- Its stated reason was that the exclusivity "has not yielded the quantity and quality of movies needed to drive demand."
- It also claimed the trial had rolled out in Seattle, Portland, Salt Lake City and New York in December, and that subscribers were buying movies.

**Analyst and press reaction (forwarded in the EBS newsletter and clippings)**
- Lehman called it "more bark than bite" and Merrill Lynch said it could accelerate Enron's content strategy.
- One analyst, however, cut EBS earnings targets to $8.40/share because of the failed deal.
- A trade newsletter said the news "unnerved investors" and sent shares from around $70 to a low of $55 on 22 March.
- EBS Europe's Steve Elliott blamed the failure on Blockbuster not securing the content Enron expected, which meant the predicted demand did not materialise.
- A June 2001 article quoted an analyst saying "no one had any earnings (from Blockbuster) in the company projections for several years at best."

**Cleanup, August 2001**
- Enron's legal staff told employees who may have been exposed to Blockbuster's confidential information to review all files and documentation and "destroy all Confidential Information in your possession immediately." The email gives no reason beyond the Master Agreement. This was before the October 2001 document-preservation order, which named EBS among its subjects (item 4 on its list).

**After the collapse, late 2001 to January 2002 (press clippings circulated inside Enron)**
- The Braveheart partnership dominated this coverage. Enron obtained a $115.2 million investment in it from CIBC World Markets.
- Enron claimed a $53 million profit from Braveheart for Q4 2000, when the Blockbuster pilot was only two weeks old and not generating profit.
- A former employee said: "How can they monetize this asset when we're still putting it together?"
- Blockbuster's spokeswoman said, "It was nothing but a pilot project. I don't know how anyone could have been booking revenues." She also said Blockbuster didn't know about Braveheart at the time.
- The October 2001 third-quarter loss included a reversal of the $110.9 million in Braveheart profits.
- Current CFO McMahon said he had nothing to do with Braveheart.

**Gaps**
- The mailbox holds little candid internal debate about the Blockbuster deal itself; most insider commentary on its merits is in the PR and newsletter material.
- The accounting claims come from press accounts, not from internal finance emails I found.

When Enron Corp. and Blockbuster Inc. joined forces in mid-2000, it looked like they were on to something big. The companies announced they would soon be allowing consumers across America to choose from among thousands of movies, including hot new features, sent via telephone lines to watch on their TVs at home. 
Announcing the partnership in July, 2000, Enron chairman Kenneth Lay called it the "killer app for the entertainment industry." Blockbuster chairman John Antioco said the two companies had come up with the "ultimate bricks-clicks-and-flicks strategy." Oracle Corp. chairman Larry Ellison later committed his private company, nCube Corp., to provide critical computer hardware and $2-million (U.S.). Mr. Ellison said he was "proud" to be part of the venture.
It looked like another brilliant move by Enron, already a hero on Wall Street. But within eight months of its launch, the partners had split. Enron's impatience "didn't add up," says Blockbuster spokeswoman Karen Raskopf. 
As it turns out, Blockbuster didn't know the half of it. Within months of inking the deal, Enron had set up an affiliated partnership, code-named Project Braveheart, an apparent allusion to the 1995 Mel Gibson movie. Enron obtained a $115.2-million investment in the partnership from CIBC World Markets, the investment-banking arm of Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce in Toronto. In return, CIBC received a promise of almost all earnings from Enron's share of the venture for the first 10 years. Blockbuster didn't know about Braveheart at the time, Ms. Raskopf says.

The partnership had no separate staff and no assets other than Enron's stake in the venture with Blockbuster, which was barely getting off the ground in late 2000. Still, in an audacious accounting move, Enron claimed $110.9-million in profits from Braveheart in the fourth quarter of 2000 and the first quarter of 2001. That amount sharply limited the overall losses suffered by Enron's fibre-optics division in the two periods. 
At its peak, in March, 2001, the venture with Blockbuster provided only about 1,000 test customers with movies in four U.S. cities. Many of those customers didn't even pay. "It was nothing but a pilot project," says Blockbuster's Ms. Raskopf. "I don't know how anyone could have been booking revenues." 
Blockbuster, a unit of Viacom Inc., never accounted for any financial gain or loss from the short-lived venture, she says. 
Project Braveheart was one of dozens of outside partnerships that Enron officials created to burnish the company's financial results at a time when it felt under pressure to show high profits that would justify its soaring stock price, according to current and former company executives. One of the reasons Enron began sliding toward bankruptcy court last fall was the abandonment of some of these accounting manoeuvres, which contributed to huge losses and the collapse of its stock. 
Some of the partnerships were designed to shift large debts off Enron's balance sheet and make the company appear more robust in the eyes of investors and credit-rating agencies. Others, such as Braveheart, raised fast cash needed to fund Enron's ever-expanding array of new businesses. 
Enron's current chief financial officer, Jeffrey McMahon, says he had nothing to do with Braveheart or related partnerships. "I'm not going to defend them," he says. An Enron spokeswoman says the company has no other comment.
